headline: Oil climbed toward $114 a barrel, near its highest since May, as Houthi attacks forced Saudi Aramco to clear its headquarters. The yen hit a one-month high, and UK retail sales fell more than expected.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The dollar index held near a three-week low around 101.5 in Asian trading. A tech-led stock sell-off has pulled US bond yields down, and traders trimmed bets on a December Federal Reserve hike to about 85%, from about 90%.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: since the US–Iran war began in February, high oil has kept US inflation up, and with it bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates again in December, which has supported the dollar. What changed: worries that heavy AI spending won't pay off knocked tech shares on Thursday, and the selling spread to Asia on Friday, with Japan's Nikkei down about 1.3%. Investors kept money in US government bonds: the 10-year yield held near 4.96%, just under 5%, and the 2-year eased to about 4.66%. December hike odds slipped to about 85%. The dollar index sat near 101.5, losing most to the yen. What it means: when markets wobble, the Fed has less need to keep raising rates, and lower US yields make the dollar less rewarding to hold. High oil still argues the other way. The question to keep asking: does the stock sell-off keep pulling yields down, or do strong US figures pull them back up?
chapters.fx: What's next: US business surveys (flash PMIs) at 8:45 AM CT today and the final University of Michigan survey, with its inflation expectations, at 9:00 AM CT. The Fed's next decision is October 28; it is in its quiet period until then.

scenarios.bull: If the surveys or inflation expectations run hot, yields climb back above 5% and the dollar firms.
scenarios.bear: If the stock sell-off spreads into Europe and New York, yields slide further and the dollar loses more ground to the yen.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro held near $1.121 in Asian trading. Coming up: business surveys for France, Germany and the euro area between 2:15 and 3:00 AM CT, then Moody's review of France's credit rating after European markets close.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the euro has been held back by France's budget fight and by expensive energy, which Europe imports. The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, because euro-area inflation is well above its 2% target. What changed: little overnight. The euro stayed near $1.121 as oil rose toward $114 a barrel. France's 10-year borrowing cost is above 5%, and its gap over Germany is near the widest since 2011. What it means: dearer oil and French debt worries weigh on the euro, while expected ECB hikes support it, so the day's surveys and Moody's decide which side gains. The question: does Moody's cut France's rating tonight?
chapters.fx: What's next: flash business surveys for France (2:15 AM CT), Germany (2:30 AM CT) and the euro area (3:00 AM CT), then Moody's review of France after European markets close. October 27: the French parliament's vote on the budget's tax side. October 29: the ECB's decision.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: UK retail sales fell 0.4% in September, worse than the 0.1% drop expected, a day after consumer confidence had its steepest fall since 2020. The pound sat near $1.339 before the figures; a Bank of England hike in November still looks all but certain.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Gulf war has pushed up energy bills, and Britain, which imports a lot of gas, has felt it more than most. UK inflation of 3.5% in September made a Bank of England hike on November 5 close to certain; the open question is a second hike in December. What changed: retail sales volumes fell 0.4% in September, against a 0.1% fall expected, as energy costs and worry about the October 28 budget held shoppers back. On Thursday evening GfK's consumer confidence index fell 11 points to −24, far below the −14 expected and its steepest drop since early 2020. What it means: shoppers are pulling back just as rates rise. That does not change November, but it weakens the case for a second hike in December, which takes some support from the pound. The question: do business surveys show the slowdown spreading?
chapters.fx: What's next: UK flash business surveys at 3:30 AM CT today. October 28: the UK budget from Chancellor John Healey. November 5: the Bank of England's decision.
numbers: UK retail sales −0.4% m/m in Sep (−0.1% expected)

scenarios.bull: If the surveys surprise higher, December hike bets recover and the pound with them.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The yen reached its strongest in over a month, with the dollar dipping to about ¥156.3 before steadying near ¥156.9. Japan's core inflation rose to 2.1%, back above the Bank of Japan's 2% goal, and stock-market jitters kept investors seeking shelter.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the yen has been the weakest major currency, because Japan's rates are far below everyone else's and Japan pays heavily for imported energy. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30 and is increasingly expected to hike in December. What changed: Japan's national core inflation rose to 2.1% in September, as expected and up from 1.7%, the first reading above the 2% goal in nine months. A broader measure that also leaves out energy jumped to 2.4%. Flash business surveys showed factories cooling but services growing. Meanwhile Japan's stocks fell, and the dollar slipped to about ¥156.3 in Asian trading. What it means: price rises are spreading beyond fuel, which is what the Bank of Japan wants to see before hiking, and fear in markets adds safe-haven buying. A lasting recovery still needs the hike itself. The question: does governor Kazuo Ueda signal December next week?
chapters.fx: What's next: no more Japanese data this week. The yen moves with stock markets and US yields into the Bank of Japan's decision on October 29–30.
numbers: USD/JPY ~156.3–156.9; yen strongest in over a month

scenarios.bull: If the stock sell-off deepens or US yields keep falling, the yen extends its gains toward ¥155.
scenarios.bear: If stocks bounce and US yields climb back above 5%, the dollar returns toward ¥158.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The franc held near a one-month high against the dollar, at about 0.821, as nervous markets kept demand for safe currencies. There is no Swiss data until next week.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Swiss franc is a safe place to park money in a crisis, but Swiss inflation is near zero, so the Swiss National Bank holds rates at 0%. On Thursday the bank's summary of its September discussion said the franc has become popular to borrow for carry trades, and it eased its readiness to step into currency markets. What changed: the dollar slipped to about 0.82 francs in Asian trading as stock markets fell. The yen, not the franc, led the rush to safety. What it means: the bank is not fighting the franc in either direction, so global fear sets its path. The question: does Gulf fear keep building over the weekend?
chapters.fx: What's next: no Swiss data until next week. The franc moves with war headlines and stock markets. December 10: the Swiss National Bank's next decision.

scenarios.bear: If fear fades and carry trades return, the franc softens.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: Australia's private sector shrank in October for the first time in five months, while business costs rose at the fastest pace since May. The Australian dollar held near 70.2 US cents as markets weighed whether that rules out a November rate hike.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Australia's inflation has picked up with energy prices, and Reserve Bank of Australia deputy governor Andrew Hauser said this week the outlook was materially worse, making a November hike close to an even bet. What changed: S&P Global's flash surveys showed overall activity falling to 47.7 in October, from 51.3, with services back below 50, the line between growth and shrinking. Input costs rose at the fastest pace since May. The Aussie held near 0.7016. What it means: slowing activity argues against a hike while rising costs argue for one, which leaves the November decision finely balanced. The question: does third-quarter inflation on October 28 settle it?
chapters.fx: What's next: no major Australian data until October 28, when third-quarter consumer prices come out. November 2–3: the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision.

scenarios.base: If stocks steady, the Australian dollar holds near 70 cents into the inflation report.
scenarios.bull: If inflation on October 28 runs hot, November hike bets rise and the Aussie climbs.
scenarios.bear: If the stock sell-off deepens or inflation cools, hike bets fade and the Aussie slips.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The loonie firmed past 1.40 per US dollar, its strongest in about a month, helped by oil near $100 for US crude. A Bank of Canada hike next Wednesday is mostly priced; Canadian retail sales come at 7:30 AM CT.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: high oil lifts Canada's export income but also its inflation. Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said the bank's inflation forecast would be revised substantially higher on energy, and markets moved to expect a hike on October 28. What changed: US crude rose to about $100 a barrel overnight as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued, and the US dollar eased to about 1.4007 Canadian. Thursday's factory and raw material prices had already jumped far more than expected. What it means: dearer oil helps the loonie twice, through export income and by firming the hike case. Much of the October hike is already in the price, so the next move depends on whether the bank signals more. The question: does Macklem hint at further hikes?
chapters.fx: What's next: Canadian retail sales for August at 7:30 AM CT today (about 1.3% expected after a 0.7% drop). October 28: the Bank of Canada's decision.

scenarios.bull: If retail sales rebound strongly or oil climbs further, bets on more hikes lift the loonie.
scenarios.bear: If calmer Gulf news knocks oil lower or retail sales disappoint, the loonie loses some support.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi steadied near 56.9 US cents after Thursday's drop, as Asian stocks slipped again. A Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 is still seen as near certain.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: New Zealand's central bank, the RBNZ, has turned toward raising rates as energy and food push inflation above its 1–3% target band. Third-quarter inflation came in at 3.7%, a touch below forecasts but still above the band. What changed: no New Zealand news overnight. The kiwi held near 0.5685, after falling about 0.5% on Thursday when tech and war fears hit stock markets. What it means: the expected hike supports the kiwi, but it is among the first currencies sold when investors get nervous. The question: does the RBNZ signal more than one hike when it meets?
chapters.fx: What's next: no major New Zealand data before the RBNZ's decision on October 28. Until then the kiwi moves with stock markets and the US dollar.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Brent crude rose about 0.5–1% to near $114 a barrel in Asian trading, on track for a third weekly gain. Saudi Aramco ordered its Dhahran headquarters evacuated as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia grew, and a pipeline shutdown cut Libyan output.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: oil has been high since the US–Iran war began in February, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut. Brent jumped about 4% on Thursday after deadly Houthi drone strikes on a Saudi oil field and airport. What changed: Saudi Aramco told staff to leave its Dhahran headquarters as fighting with the Houthis intensified, a sign the rebels can now reach deeper into Saudi Arabia. In Libya, a shut pipeline valve cut output at two oil fields. Senior Israeli military sources said no strike on Iran is planned before the November 3 US midterms. Brent rose to about $114 and US crude to about $100. What it means: the threat now sits inside Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter, so buyers keep paying a risk premium. That feeds inflation worries and helps oil exporters like Canada, while hurting importers like Japan and the euro area. The question: do attacks reach actual Saudi output?
chapters.fx: What's next: any further Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites or Red Sea shipping over the weekend, and Israel's October 27 election. The November 3 US midterms are the next big date for any US move on Iran.

scenarios.bull: If an attack cuts Saudi output or shuts more Red Sea traffic, Brent climbs well above its May highs.
scenarios.bear: If the Houthi attacks pause over the weekend, Brent eases back toward $110.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold slipped to about $4,020 an ounce in Asian trading, its lowest in about two months, extending a five-day slide. Dearer oil keeps alive the chance of more US rate hikes, and gold pays no interest.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: gold ran to records this year on war fears and central-bank buying, but it has slid for a week as markets priced a December Federal Reserve hike, since gold pays no interest. What changed: gold fell to about $4,020, below a level near $4,065 that Societe Generale strategists had seen as a floor; they now see room toward the June low near $3,950. It fell even as US yields dropped and Gulf attacks grew. What it means: gold is trading on rate expectations and on selling to cover losses elsewhere, not on war fear. Hedge funds were still strongly betting on gold in the latest US futures data, though trimming. The question: what breaks the slide, a lasting fall in rate-hike bets or a real hit to Gulf supply?
chapters.fx: What's next: US business surveys at 8:45 AM CT and the University of Michigan's inflation expectations at 9:00 AM CT. New US futures positioning data come Friday afternoon.

calls.text: France's revenue-section budget vote Tue: a clean pass narrows the French–German spread (~141bp); a defeat or big concessions widens it and weighs on the euro
calls.note: No vote on Tuesday: it was pushed to October 27, so neither branch played out.

calls.text: UK jobs Tue 1 AM CT (earnings ~3.8% expected): sticky pay firms the BoE hike case before Wednesday's inflation; cooling pay backs Bailey's calmer view
calls.note: Sticky side won: unemployment fell to 4.7% (4.9% expected) and regular pay rose 3.7% (3.6% expected); total pay and claims were softer. Pound +0.3% to ~1.334.

calls.text: Konarak follow-through: a US confirmation or more strikes keeps oil's supply premium and lifts US yields; silence lets the morning's waiver drop resume
calls.note: No confirmation (a US official denied the strike) and no new strike overnight, yet the premium held: Brent ~$109.8 Tuesday on low Gulf flows and Iran's Hormuz claims. The waiver-driven drop did not resume.

calls.text: BoC Oct 28 with ~87% priced for a hike: a hike is mostly in the loonie already; a hold would be the surprise and hit it
NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (~3.8% y/y): near forecast keeps the ~80% hike pricing; clearly soft reopens the hold and weighs on the kiwi
calls.note: Near forecast (3.7% vs 3.8%) and hike pricing held, rising to about 98%; the kiwi dipped only briefly.
